Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fission Environment CRD create/update with dangerous SecurityContext on standalone container (CVE-2026-50566) AIExploitation High
Hunts Kubernetes API audit events where a Fission Environment CRD (apiGroup fission.io) is created/updated carrying privileged, allowPrivilegeEscalation, or dangerous-capability SecurityContext specifically on the standalone spec.runtime.container / spec.builder.container fields — the exact field the round-4 PodSpec sanitiser missed. This is the earliest and highest-fidelity catch of the CVE-2026-50566 admission bypass before any pod is scheduled. Rationale: Pivots on the exact article strings: objectRef.resource=environments + apiGroup fission.io, and the standalone spec.runtime.container/spec.builder.container securityContext fields with privileged/allowPrivilegeEscalation/SYS_ADMIN/NET_ADMIN/SYS_PTRACE — the precise merge-layer gap named in the advisory PoC. Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail left empty because K8s API audit telemetry is not in those schemas. Corroborated against NVD and GitLab/CIRCL advisories. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m63v-2g9w-2w6v • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-50566 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/fission/fission/CVE-2026-50566/
ATT&CKT1611 T1610 T1548
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cluster administrator deliberately creating a debug/system Fission Environment with elevated capabilities (should be rare and reviewed)
  • GitOps controller (ArgoCD/Flux) reconciling an Environment manifest that legitimately declares NET_ADMIN for a networking function
  • Fission upgrade/CI tooling re-applying pre-existing environment definitions
  • Security team re-running the CVE-2026-50566 PoC during patch validation
  • A pre-existing (pre-patch) privileged environment being updated for an unrelated field, re-emitting the SecurityContext
Suppression filter
| where Actor !startswith "system:serviceaccount:argocd:" and Actor !startswith "system:serviceaccount:flux-system:" and Actor !endswith ":cluster-admin"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the Username/service account and sourceIPs on the audit event; confirm it is a tenant (not cluster-admin) principal and check whether the Environment name/namespace is expected. Verify cluster Fission version < 1.24.0 (vulnerable). 2) CONTAIN: Delete or revert the offending Environment CRD; revoke environments.fission.io create/update RBAC from the identity; apply a Kyverno/OPA policy rejecting dangerous container SecurityContext and label the function/builder namespace pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all pods in fission function/builder namespaces for privileged/added-capability containers (UC2); review audit logs from the same principal for exec/attach into resulting pods, node filesystem access, and secret reads indicating a completed escape.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) == "environments" and tostring(ObjectRef.apiGroup) == "fission.io"
| extend RuntimeSC = RequestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext
| extend BuilderSC = RequestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext
| where tostring(RuntimeSC.privileged) == "true"
    or tostring(BuilderSC.privileged) == "true"
    or tostring(RuntimeSC.allowPrivilegeEscalation) == "true"
    or tostring(BuilderSC.allowPrivilegeEscalation) == "true"
    or tostring(RuntimeSC.capabilities.add) has_any ("SYS_ADMIN","NET_ADMIN","SYS_PTRACE")
    or tostring(BuilderSC.capabilities.add) has_any ("SYS_ADMIN","NET_ADMIN","SYS_PTRACE")
| project TimeGenerated, Verb, Actor = Username, Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), EnvName = tostring(ObjectRef.name), RuntimeSC, BuilderSC, UserAgent, SourceIPs = RequestObject.spec
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Fission Environment CRD Privileged Standalone Container SecurityContext (CVE-2026-50566)
id: 6f3b1c8a-2d4e-4a91-9b7c-8e1a2f5c9d20
description: Detects create/update of a Fission Environment CRD whose standalone runtime.container or builder.container SecurityContext requests privileged, allowPrivilegeEscalation, or dangerous Linux capabilities, bypassing the PodSpec-only admission validation.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m63v-2g9w-2w6v
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-50566
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:
  - attack.t1611
  - attack.t1610
  - attack.t1548
logsource:
  product: kubernetes
  service: audit
detection:
  selection_resource:
    verb:
      - create
      - update
      - patch
    objectRef.resource: environments
    objectRef.apiGroup: fission.io
  selection_priv:
    requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.privileged: true
  selection_bpriv:
    requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.privileged: true
  selection_ape:
    requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: true
  selection_bape:
    requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: true
  selection_caps:
    requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.capabilities.add|contains:
      - SYS_ADMIN
      - NET_ADMIN
      - SYS_PTRACE
  selection_bcaps:
    requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.capabilities.add|contains:
      - SYS_ADMIN
      - NET_ADMIN
      - SYS_PTRACE
  condition: selection_resource and (selection_priv or selection_bpriv or selection_ape or selection_bape or selection_caps or selection_bcaps)
level: high
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update OR patch) @objectRef.resource:environments @objectRef.apiGroup:fission.io (@requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.privileged:true OR @requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.privileged:true OR @requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation:true OR @requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation:true OR @requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.capabilities.add:(SYS_ADMIN OR NET_ADMIN OR SYS_PTRACE) OR @requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.capabilities.add:(SYS_ADMIN OR NET_ADMIN OR SYS_PTRACE))
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" (verb=create OR verb=update OR verb=patch) objectRef.resource=environments objectRef.apiGroup=fission.io
| spath output=priv path=requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.privileged
| spath output=bpriv path=requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.privileged
| spath output=ape path=requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation
| spath output=bape path=requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation
| spath output=caps path=requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.capabilities.add{}
| spath output=bcaps path=requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.capabilities.add{}
| where priv="true" OR bpriv="true" OR ape="true" OR bape="true" OR match(caps,"SYS_ADMIN|NET_ADMIN|SYS_PTRACE") OR match(bcaps,"SYS_ADMIN|NET_ADMIN|SYS_PTRACE")
| table _time user.username objectRef.namespace objectRef.name priv bpriv ape bape caps bcaps sourceIPs{}
| sort - _time
Privileged / dangerous-capability pod scheduled in Fission function/builder namespace by executor SA AIInstallation Medium
Defence-in-depth for CVE-2026-50566: catches the resulting pod when the Fission executor/buildermgr service account schedules a pod containing a privileged, allowPrivilegeEscalation, or dangerous-capability container. Fires even if a future variant uses a different bypass field, because it inspects the actual materialised Pod SecurityContext rather than the Environment CRD. Rationale: Targets the materialised outcome described in the impact section: a privileged/dangerous-capability container scheduled under the executor's high-privilege service account (system:serviceaccount:fission*) or bearing the fission environmentName label. Complements UC1 by inspecting the Pod SecurityContext directly, so it survives field-name variants of the bypass. K8s-audit-only telemetry, hence Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m63v-2g9w-2w6v • https://www.thehackerwire.com/fission-critical-container-escape-and-privilege-escalation-cve-2026-50566/
ATT&CKT1610 T1611
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately privileged Fission system component if the operator intentionally runs one (verify against Fission Helm values)
  • Node-level DaemonSets sharing the fission namespace that legitimately require NET_ADMIN
  • Third-party admission mutating webhook injecting a privileged sidecar into fission pods
  • Migration/upgrade jobs run by the fission executor SA during a version bump
  • Cluster monitoring agent pod co-scheduled in the fission namespace with SYS_PTRACE for profiling
Suppression filter
| where ContainerName !in ("fission-fetcher") and PodGenerateName !startswith "fission-upgrade"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the pod's ownerReference/environmentName label ties it to a Fission Environment, and cross-reference UC1 to see which Environment CRD produced it; note the executor SA and namespace. 2) CONTAIN: Delete the pod and its parent Environment/Deployment; cordon the node it landed on and inspect for host mount or hostPID/hostNetwork abuse; rotate any secrets reachable from that namespace. 3) HUNT: kubectl-audit for exec/attach into the pod, and check node auditd/EDR for container-escape indicators (writes to /proc, host filesystem access, nsenter). Sweep all fission namespaces for other privileged pods and enumerate identities holding environments.fission.io create/update RBAC.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb == "create" and tostring(ObjectRef.resource) == "pods"
| where Username startswith "system:serviceaccount:fission" or isnotempty(tostring(RequestObject.metadata.labels.environmentName))
| mv-expand Container = RequestObject.spec.containers
| extend SC = Container.securityContext
| where tostring(SC.privileged) == "true"
    or tostring(SC.allowPrivilegeEscalation) == "true"
    or tostring(SC.capabilities.add) has_any ("SYS_ADMIN","NET_ADMIN","SYS_PTRACE")
| project TimeGenerated, ExecutorSA = Username, Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), PodGenerateName = tostring(RequestObject.metadata.generateName), EnvLabel = tostring(RequestObject.metadata.labels.environmentName), ContainerName = tostring(Container.name), SC
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:create @objectRef.resource:pods (@user.username:system\:serviceaccount\:fission* OR @requestObject.metadata.labels.environmentName:*) (@requestObject.spec.containers.securityContext.privileged:true OR @requestObject.spec.containers.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation:true OR @requestObject.spec.containers.securityContext.capabilities.add:(SYS_ADMIN OR NET_ADMIN OR SYS_PTRACE))
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" verb=create objectRef.resource=pods
| spath output=fissionEnv path=requestObject.metadata.labels.environmentName
| spath output=fissionUid path=requestObject.metadata.labels{}
| search (user.username="system:serviceaccount:fission*" OR fissionEnv=*)
| spath output=priv path=requestObject.spec.containers{}.securityContext.privileged
| spath output=ape path=requestObject.spec.containers{}.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation
| spath output=caps path=requestObject.spec.containers{}.securityContext.capabilities.add{}
| where priv="true" OR ape="true" OR match(caps,"SYS_ADMIN|NET_ADMIN|SYS_PTRACE")
| table _time user.username objectRef.namespace requestObject.metadata.generateName fissionEnv priv ape caps
| sort - _time

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ToddyCat: your hidden email assistant. Part 2

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-06-30 11 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An in-depth analysis of Umbrij, a new tool used by the ToddyCat APT group to compromise corporate email communications in Gmail. The attack targeted OAuth authorization tokens, allowing threat actors to gain access to Google services.

ATT&CKT1027 T1053.005 T1134.003 T1190 T1204.002 T1528 T1574.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Umbrij command-line switches (-deepsearch / -runas-currentuser / -debugport / -domainAd / -savepdf) · [LLM] Chromium browser launched headless with --remote-debugging-port by a non-browser parent (STRD) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ToddyCat: your hidden email assistant. Part 2
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Masquerading scheduled task 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' launching a signed binary · [LLM] ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-loading: signed host loading malicious log.dll/GoogleServices.dll from writable path · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Sideload-host binary connecting to Google OAuth/Gmail API endpoints (token exchange) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Masquerading scheduled task 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' launching a signed binary AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence/launch step where ToddyCat created a scheduled task named KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp to run a digitally-signed sideload host. Kaspersky never creates a task with this name, so any occurrence of the string is malicious by definition. Rationale: Anchors on the exact masquerading task name 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' called out in the article's Execution section; it is a fixed, unique string no legitimate product emits. Cross-checked Securelist part 2 and the ToddyCat series. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-steals-email-data-from-outlook/118044/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A SOC analyst manually re-creating the task name during IR reproduction/testing
  • An internal red-team emulating ToddyCat TTPs
  • A detection-content lab importing the IOC string into a test task
  • Documentation/scripts that reference the task name in comments being scanned by inventory tooling
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the scheduled task definition (Actions/Exec path) and the signed binary it launches; verify the signer and whether the path is a writable dir (Users\Public, Temp, vss). 2) Contain: disable/delete the task, isolate the host, and capture the launched binary + any same-folder DLL for analysis. 3) Hunt: pivot on the launched binary hash and folder across the fleet; check for the BDS.exe/log.dll sideload chain and Chromium remote-debugging launches on the same host within +/- 1h.
union
(DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ProcessCommandLine has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Evidence=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName),
(DeviceRegistryEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RegistryKey has @"\TaskCache\" and RegistryKey has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Evidence=RegistryKey, InitiatingProcessFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4698, 4702, 4699)
| where EventData has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, Activity, EventID, EventData
title: Masquerading Scheduled Task KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp (ToddyCat Umbrij)
id: 6f3a1d2e-9b7c-4e10-8a44-2c1f0b9d7e51
description: Detects creation or reference to a scheduled task named KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp, a name ToddyCat used to masquerade Umbrij launch. Kaspersky does not create tasks with this name.

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i | CommandLine=/KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-loading: signed host loading malicious log.dll/GoogleServices.dll from writable path AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact sideload pairs ToddyCat abused to launch Umbrij: BDSubWiz.exe/bds.exe loading log.dll, VSTestVideoRecorder.exe loading Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll, and GoogleDesktop.exe loading GoogleServices.dll, when the module loads from a user-writable directory or matches the known log.dll hashes. Rationale: Uses the exact legitimate-host -> malicious-DLL pairs named in the article (BDSubWiz/bds.exe+log.dll, VSTestVideoRecorder+VideoRecorderEngine.dll, GoogleDesktop+GoogleServices.dll), plus the writable paths and log.dll/BDS.exe MD5s read directly from in-article screenshot image1.jpeg (4C39087.../22AAEB49... and 28CB7B26...). Writable-path constraint removes legitimate in-product loads. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2026/06/16200713/image1.jpeg • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Bitdefender ConnectAgent running BDSubWiz.exe from its real Program Files path (excluded by writable-path filter)
  • Visual Studio test runs loading VideoRecorderEngine.dll from the VS install directory
  • A legacy Google Desktop install in Program Files loading GoogleServices.dll
  • Security testing/EDR validation copying these binaries into a sandbox temp folder
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loaded DLL hash against the known IOCs and verify the host binary is running from Users\Public/Temp/vss rather than its vendor install path; check the DLL export (LogInit) and ConfuserEx markers. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the DLL and host binary, kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: from the host process, pivot to child Chromium launches with --remote-debugging-port and outbound connections to *.googleapis.com; sweep fleet for the same DLL hashes and the KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp task.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe") and FileName =~ "log.dll")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" and FileName =~ "Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "GoogleDesktop.exe" and FileName =~ "GoogleServices.dll")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Windows\vss\")
     or MD5 in~ ("4C39087E5229A70F0215AFB8B7083091","22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, Dll=FileName, DllPath=FolderPath, MD5, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\BDSubWiz.exe", @"\bds.exe", @"\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe", @"\GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Windows\vss\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Umbrij command-line switches (-deepsearch / -runas-currentuser / -debugport / -domainAd / -savepdf) AIExploitation High
Hunts execution of the Umbrij tool by its distinctive command-line parameters documented in the article, including the example invocation of a renamed BDSubWiz.exe with -regex and -deepsearch. These switch names are unique to Umbrij. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim Umbrij CLI parameters enumerated in the article's parameter table (-deepsearch, -runas-currentuser, -domainAd, -savepdf, -debugport, -browser). These switch spellings are tool-specific and not used by mainstream software, giving very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/
ATT&CKT1528 T1134.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A bespoke internal automation tool that happens to use a -debugport plus -browser flag combination
  • Red-team replaying Umbrij invocations during an authorized engagement
  • An unrelated CLI utility using the generic -savepdf flag (mitigated by requiring the ToddyCat-specific switch set)
  • Developer testing of a custom .NET tool with similar argument naming
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and the executing binary; resolve which browser/path/port were targeted (-path, -browser, -debugport) and whether -runas-currentuser/-user indicates token impersonation. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and revoke/rotate the affected user's Google OAuth sessions and tokens immediately. 3) Hunt: correlate with the parent sideload host (BDS.exe/log.dll), Chromium --remote-debugging-port launches, and outbound *.googleapis.com traffic on the same host and account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-deepsearch","-runas-currentuser","-domainAd","-savepdf")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "-debugport" and ProcessCommandLine has "-browser")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("-deepsearch","-runas-currentuser","-domainAd","-savepdf")
   or (CommandLine has "-debugport" and CommandLine has "-browser")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Chromium browser launched headless with --remote-debugging-port by a non-browser parent (STRD) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the core Shadow-Token-via-Remote-Debug step: Umbrij launches Chrome/Edge/Chromium with a remote debugging port (often headless) to drive the user's live Gmail session. Flags browser processes carrying --remote-debugging-port when spawned by the sideload hosts or run headless. Rationale: Built on the article's explicit description of launching a Chromium browser in headless mode and connecting via the remote debugging port; pairs the --remote-debugging-port flag with the article-specific sideload parents or the --headless evasion flag to suppress legitimate interactive debugging. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1185 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers/QA running Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright automation with --remote-debugging-port and --headless
  • CI build agents driving headless Chrome for screenshot or PDF generation
  • VS Code / IDE debugging a web app via the Chrome DevTools Protocol
  • Synthetic monitoring agents launching headless browsers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft VS Code" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","devenv.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and folder — a CI/automation tool from a dev path is likely benign; a browser spawned by BDSubWiz/bds/GoogleDesktop or from Users\Public/Temp is malicious. Note the --remote-debugging-port value and target profile. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the browser and parent, and immediately revoke the user's Google sessions/refresh tokens and force re-auth. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound *.googleapis.com / accounts.google.com connections from the same host/account and to the Umbrij CLI-switch and log.dll sideload detections.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","chromium.exe","brave.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
     or ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\chrome.exe", @"\msedge.exe", @"\chromium.exe", @"\brave.exe")
| where CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ParentProcessName has_any (@"\BDSubWiz.exe", @"\bds.exe", @"\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe", @"\GoogleDesktop.exe")
     or CommandLine has "--headless"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: Chromium Remote Debugging Port Launch by Non-Browser Parent (ToddyCat STRD)
id: 4a8c6b29-1e57-4d33-9b2a-0f7e5c3a1d92
description: Detects Chrome/Edge/Chromium launched with --remote-debugging-port either headless or spawned by a ToddyCat sideload-host binary, the core of the Shadow Token via Remote Debug technique.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.t1185
  - attack.t1528
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  browser_debug:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\chromium.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '--remote-debugging-port'

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\MSEdge.exe OR *\\chromium.exe)) @CommandLine:*--remote-debugging-port* (@CommandLine:*--headless* OR @ParentImage:(*\\BDS.exe OR *\\bds.exe OR *\\BDSubWiz.exe OR *\\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe OR *\\GoogleDesktop.exe))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|chromium|brave)\.exe$/i CommandLine=/--remote-debugging-port/i | (CommandLine=/--headless/i OR ParentBaseFileName=/(BDSubWiz|bds|VSTestVideoRecorder|GoogleDesktop)\.exe$/i) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="chrome.exe" OR Processes.process_name="msedge.exe" OR Processes.process_name="chromium.exe") AND Processes.process="*--remote-debugging-port*" AND (Processes.process="*--headless*" OR Processes.parent_process_name="BDSubWiz.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="bds.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="GoogleDesktop.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Sideload-host binary connecting to Google OAuth/Gmail API endpoints (token exchange) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access/exfil step where Umbrij (running as a renamed signed binary, not a browser) exchanges the stolen OAuth authorization code for an access token and pulls Gmail via the Google API. Flags the sideload hosts contacting *.googleapis.com / accounts.google.com. Rationale: Combines the article's OAuth-code-to-access-token exchange and Google-API access with the sideload host names confirmed in screenshot image1.jpeg; a renamed Bitdefender/VSTest/GoogleDesktop binary speaking directly to Google OAuth/Gmail APIs (work normally done only by the browser) is a strong, low-FP anomaly. Sentinel left empty because process-attributed network telemetry to these hosts is not available in standard Sentinel tables (would require Sysmon EID3 ingestion). Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2026/06/16200713/image1.jpeg • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1528 T1114.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Google Desktop legacy install (in Program Files) performing update/sync checks to googleapis.com
  • Bitdefender ConnectAgent telemetry/update traffic to a Google-hosted CDN (rare; mitigated by host-name + writable-path context)
  • Security testing of the binaries in a lab with live internet
  • A renamed-but-benign internal tool reusing one of these file names
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating binary path/signer and verify it is the renamed sideload host rather than the genuine vendor product; pull the destination URLs and timing relative to any browser remote-debug launch. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the binary, and revoke the affected Google account's OAuth tokens/refresh tokens and active sessions; review Google Workspace audit logs for token grants and bulk message reads. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts where these binaries reach Google APIs, correlate with the log.dll sideload and KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp task, and check for mailbox data staged/exfiltrated.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oauth2.googleapis.com","accounts.google.com","www.googleapis.com","gmail.googleapis.com","googleapis.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oauth2.googleapis.com","accounts.google.com","www.googleapis.com","gmail.googleapis.com","googleapis.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: e7b3c91d-5a42-4f8e-8c01-9d2f6a3b7e58

// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union

        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or SHA1 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or MD5 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66")

let BadHashes = dynamic(["1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen network sniffing via netsh trace capture redirected to ADMIN$ share AIReconnaissance High
Hunts The Gentlemen's reconnaissance technique of running netsh trace packet capture and writing the .etl output across the network to a remote host's ADMIN$ share. The redirect of a netsh trace start/stop session to \\<ip>\ADMIN$\ is highly specific to this actor's credential-harvesting-from-the-wire workflow. Rationale: Built from the article's exact commands 'netsh trace start capture=yes report=no filemode=circular overwrite=yes maxSize=4 > \\<target IP>\ADMIN$\{RANDOM}' and the matching 'netsh trace stop' redirect. netsh trace + ADMIN$ redirect is rare in benign admin use, making this high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps
ATT&CKT1040 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network engineer running netsh trace for legitimate troubleshooting and saving to a local file (no ADMIN$ redirect)
  • Endpoint support tooling that captures ETL traces locally
  • Microsoft support diagnostic scripts (TSS toolkit) invoking netsh trace
  • Vendor performance-monitoring agents starting circular ETW captures
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\TSS\\", "TSSv2") and AccountName endswith "admin")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the redirect target — a \\<remote-ip>\ADMIN$ path means cross-host write, not local troubleshooting. Identify the executing account and whether it is an admin/service account that does not normally run netsh. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the source host, reset the credentials of the executing account, and pull the dropped .etl from the target ADMIN$ share for analysis (it may contain cleartext creds). 3) HUNT: Search for SharpADWS/NetScan/Advanced IP Scanner activity, the deploy_gpo.ps1 script, and connections to 81.177.215.15:9443 on the same hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "netsh" and ProcessCommandLine has "trace"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("capture=yes", @"\ADMIN$\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has "netsh" and CommandLine has "trace"
| where CommandLine has_any ("capture=yes", "\\ADMIN$\\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen Go backdoor C2 beacon to 81.177.215.15 on TCP/9443 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host establishing an outbound connection to the confirmed Gentlemen Go-backdoor C2 IP 81.177.215.15 on port 9443, the Yamux-multiplexed persistent channel used for remote command execution and SOCKS proxying. Single confirmed C2 indicator deployed a day before ransomware. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit C2 endpoint 81.177.215.15:9443 for the Yamux-based Go backdoor. A hardcoded malicious IP+port is a high-confidence, near-zero-FP network IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/ • https://s2w.inc/en/resource/detail/1053
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers/sandbox detonating the sample from corporate ranges
  • Threat-intel scanning or Shodan-style internet measurement hitting the IP
  • Reused VPS IP later assigned to a benign service (validate against current TI reputation)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — a Go binary in an unusual path (Temp/Public/AppData) deployed ~1 day prior is the backdoor. Capture its SHA256 against the article's hash list. 2) CONTAIN: Network-isolate the host, block 81.177.215.15 at the perimeter, and kill/quarantine the implant binary. 3) HUNT: Look for WMI query 'SELECT UUID FROM Win32_ComputerSystemProduct', cmd.exe /c children of the implant (operator command 'c'), SOCKS proxy listeners, and expect ransomware staging within ~24h.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "81.177.215.15" and RemotePort == 9443
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "81.177.215.15" and DstPortNumber == 9443
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen BYOVD vulnerable driver drop/load (EDR-killer drivers) AIInstallation High
Hunts for the specific vulnerable kernel drivers The Gentlemen abuse in their BYOVD/GentleKiller workflow to terminate security products. Matches on the named .sys files being written or loaded, e.g. biontdrv.sys, wamsdk.sys, ProcessMonitorDriver.sys. Rationale: Driver names taken verbatim from the article's vulnerable-driver table (Safetica, WatchDog, Paragon biontdrv, inpoutx64, etc.). ESET's GentleKiller research corroborates these as the actor's BYOVD arsenal. Medium FP because inpoutx64.sys/biontdrv.sys also appear in legitimate software. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • biontdrv.sys present from a genuine Paragon Partition Manager install
  • gamedriverx64.sys from a legitimately installed game with anti-cheat
  • Security product (Safetica) itself loading ProcessMonitorDriver.sys in an authorized deployment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","paragon.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Check the signing status and the parent process that wrote/loaded the driver — a driver dropped to a non-standard path by a non-installer process is malicious; a vendor MSI installer is likely benign. Confirm whether the matching legitimate product is actually installed. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, stop the driver service, and quarantine the .sys + the loading process; verify EDR/AV agents are still running. 3) HUNT: Correlate with Set-MpPreference tampering, OpenArk64/PowerRun.exe execution, and the 81.177.215.15 C2 on the same host to confirm Gentlemen activity.

The Gentlemen impair defenses via Set-MpPreference exclusions and AV-removal tooling AIInstallation High
Detects The Gentlemen's defense-evasion step that disables Defender real-time/CFA protection, adds whole-drive exclusions via Set-MpPreference/Add-MpPreference, and runs known AV-removal utilities (kavrmvr.exe, OpenArk64, PowerRun.exe, Allpatch2.exe). Pairs the Go-implant PowerShell cmdlets with named tampering binaries. Rationale: Combines the article's verbatim Go-implant cmdlets (Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring, -EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled, Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess/-ExclusionPath 'C:\') with named tools kavrmvr.exe (Kaspersky uninstaller) and OpenArk64; PowerRun.exe/Allpatch2.exe added from corroborating Trend Micro reporting on the same actor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin legitimately adding a Defender exclusion for a line-of-business app (single ExclusionPath, not C:\)
  • Sanctioned migration off Kaspersky running kavrmvr.exe with change-ticket approval
  • Performance team disabling Real-Time Monitoring temporarily during a benchmark
  • Software packaging/SCCM scripts setting exclusions for an installer
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "ExclusionPath" and ProcessCommandLine !has @"'C:\'" and ProcessCommandLine !has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the exclusion scope — a whole-drive 'C:\' exclusion or DisableRealtimeMonitoring chained with ExclusionProcess is malicious; a narrow app path may be benign. Identify the parent process (Go implant / cmd.exe /c). 2) CONTAIN: Re-enable Defender real-time protection and CFA, remove rogue exclusions, isolate the host, and reset the executing account. 3) HUNT: Pivot to BYOVD driver loads, registry Defender-policy keys, deploy_gpo.ps1, and the 81.177.215.15 C2 to scope the intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName in~ ("kavrmvr.exe","OpenArk64.exe","PowerRun.exe","Allpatch2.exe"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
        and ProcessCommandLine has "MpPreference"
        and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled","ExclusionProcess","ExclusionPath"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

        and CommandLine has_any ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled","ExclusionProcess","ExclusionPath"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen Windows Defender disabled via Policy registry keys AIInstallation High
Detects The Gentlemen disabling Defender by writing the policy registry values DisableAntiSpyware / DisableBehaviorMonitoring / DisableOnAccessProtection / DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable = 1 under the Windows Defender policy hive (via .reg import). Distinct registry-telemetry pivot from the PowerShell-based tampering. Rationale: Registry keys and values are taken verbatim from the article's exported .reg block under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender. Value-name + data=1 under the policy hive is high-fidelity tampering. Falcon left empty: these policy keys are not reliably captured by the AsepValueUpdate (autostart) event the FDR exposes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps • https://s2w.inc/en/resource/detail/1053
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Group Policy legitimately disabling Defender on hosts managed by a third-party AV (DisableAntiSpyware pushed by GPO)
  • Gold-image build process turning off Defender before installing the enterprise AV
  • Admin troubleshooting an AV conflict by temporarily setting DisableBehaviorMonitoring
  • MDM/SCCM baseline applying a Defender configuration
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","svchost.exe","ccmexec.exe","WmiPrvSE.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether a sanctioned GPO/MDM pushed the value (InitiatingProcess = svchost/gpscript) versus an interactive process like reg.exe/regedit/cmd.exe run by a user. Check if a different enterprise AV is the intended owner. 2) CONTAIN: Revert the registry values, force a gpupdate, isolate the host if the writer was interactive/non-admin. 3) HUNT: Correlate same-host BYOVD driver loads, Set-MpPreference tampering, and C2 to 81.177.215.15:9443; expect ransomware staging shortly after.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender"
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("DisableAntiSpyware","DisableBehaviorMonitoring","DisableOnAccessProtection","DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable")
| where RegistryValueData == "1"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender"
| where RegistryValue in~ ("DisableAntiSpyware","DisableBehaviorMonitoring","DisableOnAccessProtection","DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable")
| where RegistryValueData in ("1","0x1","DWORD (0x00000001)")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen ransomware deployment via deploy_gpo.ps1 / NETLOGON staging AIActions on Objectives High
Detects The Gentlemen's domain-wide lateral movement: execution of the custom deploy_gpo.ps1 GPO-deployment script and staging of the ransomware executable on the NETLOGON share for simultaneous distribution to domain hosts. Rationale: Uses the article's named lateral-movement script deploy_gpo.ps1 and the NETLOGON-share distribution method. The deploy_gpo.ps1 filename is unique to this actor; NETLOGON-staged .exe execution corroborated by SOC Prime and Trend Micro GPO-abuse reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://socprime.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-detection/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html
ATT&CKT1484.001 T1570
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate logon-script .exe staged in NETLOGON (e.g. drive-mapping or inventory tool) executed at user logon
  • AD admin running a sanctioned GPO-deployment PowerShell script with a different name (excluded by deploy_gpo.ps1 specificity)
  • Software-distribution tooling that copies installers into SYSVOL/NETLOGON
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has @"\NETLOGON\" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("userinit.exe","gpscript.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("logon.exe","mapdrives","inventory"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open deploy_gpo.ps1 / the NETLOGON-staged binary and hash it against the article's ransomware MD5 list; identify the privileged account and source DC that staged it. 2) CONTAIN: Remove the malicious GPO and the NETLOGON/SYSVOL payload immediately, disable the abused account, and block the ransomware hash org-wide before logon-driven execution spreads. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all hosts that pulled the NETLOGON object, check for PsExec-based execution of the same binary, BYOVD driver loads, and shadow-copy deletion as pre-encryption signals.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "deploy_gpo.ps1"
    or (ProcessCommandLine has @"\NETLOGON\" and ProcessCommandLine has ".exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has "deploy_gpo.ps1"
    or (CommandLine has "\\NETLOGON\\" and CommandLine has ".exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: The Gentlemen deploy_gpo.ps1 / NETLOGON Ransomware Staging
id: f08b6e21-4c39-4a7d-9b50-3e2a1d7c6b04
description: Detects execution of the Gentlemen custom deploy_gpo.ps1 GPO-deployment script or execution of binaries staged on the NETLOGON share for domain-wide ransomware distribution.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/the-gentlemen-raas/120447/
  - https://socprime.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-detection/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/29
tags:
  - attack.t1484.001
  - attack.t1570
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_script:
    CommandLine|contains: 'deploy_gpo.ps1'
  selection_netlogon:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '\NETLOGON\'
      - '.exe'
  condition: selection_script or selection_netlogon
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 (@CommandLine:*deploy_gpo.ps1* OR (@CommandLine:*\NETLOGON\* AND @CommandLine:*.exe*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (CommandLine=/deploy_gpo\.ps1/i OR (CommandLine=/\\NETLOGON\\/i CommandLine=/\.exe/i))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*deploy_gpo.ps1*" OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*\\NETLOGON\\*" AND Processes.process="*.exe*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*deploy_gpo.ps1*" OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*\\NETLOGON\\*" AND Processes.process="*.exe*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("81.177.215.15") or RemoteUrl has_any ("live.sysinternals.com", "domain.com")

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: |

let BadHashes = dynamic(["3B46A729DB7AE6AF8B19711C9452194D", "02944C8A5535CDB5B2CBB893DB2D5ACF", "10CA9A4040001560D053B7E7885C1B95", "3C471EBC947CDF32240A90FFADF49B13", "4BE8BB62F0EBBCF4CE52C35AB6F794F5", "53C616677BC7E2A0A03127F19166D007", "5C3B9821FC82A9028CB63B9671950919", "5F0B2C6D9F442754258BF4DD841C8341", "608FAF58353B65C45EF9833358AC3787", "6AE7C9A7EA0B8C40A64225734F6BD01D", "846DC77C1246DB20D976346E0E359502", "ADAC9984B3CC43D66A0D33079BBEC299", "AE0E536766788478263BF448A9381641", "B3E418D30312C1B2C58A791286868F42", "C2764744DCB4B0E1DB79CA1E8BF65368", "D12A5B36DD00586CC374A1CAE43EFED4", "D2F72897E8986303D5567EB2384932B8", "DE1522F9219497632F30F8A6E72F26B6", "FDAE2BEB813778B4540A997706862096", "B9986A0F1F1F1A798DC3F0C59A80A1A3", "554E699C96B332468F1AE69C1AE81EF9", "5761BD63DA03686FC480245DA7BD1E9F", "B6B51508AD6F462C45FE102C85D246C8", "8F0577D28C4FF5F71B149F444BFABA8E", "525EF6014F0EF20E44FE47C1D9980B69", "407B6A136BBAA7172EB44EF9D08BB58A", "9321A61A25C7961D9F36852ECAA86F55", "73F0A8C3EA794A04E80C32038249F044", "EEF8A950952696B018AA9C6DA2F5D7AD", "EDB1C480295250DD1A38F3AA1357DEAE", "5537C708EDB9A2C21F88E34E8A0F1744"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

CISA KEV: CVE-2026-48558 — SimpleHelp Authentication Bypass Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-06-29 1 use case 0 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

SimpleHelp contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the OIDC authentication flow. When OIDC authentication is configured, identity tokens submitted during login are accepted without verifying their cryptographic signature. In a vulnerable configuration, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can submit a forged token containing arbitrary identity claims to obtain a fully authenticated technician session. In some configurations, this may also allow bypass of multi-factor authentication. Vendor: SimpleHelp , Product: SimpleHelp. Federal patch due: 2026-07-02.
